question: Today is 5 September 2026. I live in England. On 25 August I bought a new laptop for £799 in a UK retailer’s physical shop, for my personal use, and paid that retailer directly by debit card. The retailer delivered it on 27 August. From its first ordinary use it repeatedly shut down. I followed the instructions and have not damaged or modified it. On 1 September I emailed the retailer describing the fault and clearly saying I rejected the laptop and wanted a full refund. I have not agreed to repair or replacement. The retailer says it only gives store credit and I should contact the manufacturer. The laptop is available for collection, and I have kept my order confirmation and emails. Can I insist on a money refund, who is responsible, and what should I do next? Apply English law on these dates, explain important qualifications, and use OSCOLA citations. About 450 words.
expected_issues: Do not ask for dates, location, purpose or remedy election already supplied
Apply satisfactory quality and short-term rejection to the stated facts without treating fault as proven adjudication
Relate delivery and express rejection dates without inventing a statutory deadline
Trader responsibility and same-payment-method refund unless expressly agreed otherwise; no refund fee
Refund without undue delay and within 14 days from trader agreement of entitlement, not automatically from the email
Collection/return agreement and reasonable return costs with the statutory exception
Consumer cannot be forced into store credit by retailer policy; distinguish repair election without treating it as already agreed
Practical written follow-up and preserve the stated records; do not invent evidence
No distance cancellation inference for the expressly in-store purchase
405–495 substantive words, exact per-claim support, no fabricated facts or authorities
review: Same-provider AI review plus host factual/citation/length/provenance checks; no professional legal sign-off
